lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5, which feature helps someone who cannot hear a video? (Captions: the words written on the screen.) Today: designing programs that everyone can use.
Usability means people can do what they came to do quickly, without mistakes or help. Good design is clear and the same everywhere, shows that a tap worked, and stops mistakes before they happen.
Accessibility means designing for everyone: big buttons for shaky hands, strong contrast for weak or tired eyes, words read aloud, captions, and colour never the only signal.
Worked example: this planner shows tasks done or not with green and red dots only. Someone who cannot tell red from green is stuck. The fix: a tick and the word done as well.
Contrast guides say ordinary text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 with its background. The School's cards use dark ink on light paper and can read every card aloud.
User testing: give real users a task, watch quietly, ask them to think aloud, and count how many finish and how long it takes. Fix the worst problem, then test again.
In 1824 Louis Braille (1809-1852), blind from childhood and aged 15, made letters of raised dots that a fingertip reads fast. Good design starts with the people who will use it.
Try it in the world: ask someone to use an app you know, thinking aloud, and note where they get stuck. In LIFE, Success Stories acts out Louis Braille's story. Next: computing and society.

exercises.prompt: What is the problem with this screen?
choices: the buttons are too small to tap
exercises.hint: Imagine pressing the add button with a thumb.
exercises.explain: The buttons and words are tiny, so they are hard to read and to tap.

exercises.prompt: What is the problem with this screen?
choices: the text is too pale to read
exercises.hint: Look at how the words stand out from the background.
exercises.explain: Pale grey on white has too little contrast, so the words are hard to read.

exercises.prompt: Colour should never be the only way a screen shows something.
exercises.hint: Think of someone who cannot tell red from green.
exercises.explain: True: add a word, a tick or an icon, so everyone can tell.

exercises.prompt: Match each need to a feature that helps.
matches: a word or icon as well
exercises.hint: Ask what each person cannot do, then what does it another way.
exercises.explain: Captions for hearing, reading aloud for seeing, big buttons for shaky hands and words or icons for colour.

exercises.prompt: 7 of 10 users finished a task. What percentage finished?
What is the problem with this screen?
choices: too many things fight for attention
the buttons are too far apart
exercises.hint: Where does your eye go first?
exercises.explain: Adverts and coloured boxes pull the eye away from the tasks: it is cluttered.

exercises.prompt: What is the problem with this screen?
choices: the icons have no words, so users must guess
exercises.hint: Could a new user tell what each row and button means?
exercises.explain: Icons alone can mean different things to different people; a word with each makes it clear.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a user test in order.
items: watch a user try it, thinking aloud
count who finished and how long
exercises.hint: Test first, then fix, then check the fix.
exercises.explain: Choose a task, watch, measure, fix the worst problem, then test again to check.

exercises.prompt: Does it help people use the app, or make it harder?
items: a back button in the same place
exercises.hint: Imagine someone short of time, or who cannot see well.
exercises.explain: Big buttons, a back button that stays put and reading aloud help; pale text and flashing adverts get in the way.

exercises.prompt: A contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 is the usual least for ordinary text.
exercises.hint: Remember the guide for ordinary text.
exercises.explain: True: guides ask for at least 4.5 to 1 between ordinary text and its background.

exercises.prompt: Users took 30, 50, 40 and 60 seconds. What was the mean time in seconds?
exercises.hint: Add them, then share by how many users there were.

exercises.prompt: Design A: 12 of 20 users finished. Design B: 18 of 20. How many percentage points better is B?
Testers keep tapping the title, thinking it goes back. What is the best fix?
choices: add a clear back button where they look
tell users to read the help
exercises.hint: Design for what users really do.
exercises.explain: Users expect to go back there, so put a clear back button in that place.

exercises.prompt: Testing with only the designer is as good as testing with real users.
exercises.hint: Does the designer already know how it works?
exercises.explain: False: the designer knows the app, so they miss what confuses new users; real users show the problems.

exercises.prompt: Label the parts of the planner's screen.
exercises.hint: Start with what you would tap to go back, then read down the screen.
exercises.explain: The back button is top left by the title; the task list is in the middle; the add button is at the bottom.

exercises.prompt: Why did Louis Braille's dots work better than huge raised letters?
choices: a fingertip feels a small group of dots fast
exercises.hint: Think about what a fingertip can feel at once.
exercises.explain: A letter of a few dots fits under one fingertip, so reading is fast; huge letters had to be traced slowly.
